items.title: The [blank] pocalypse
items.content:
It’s really just the suffix doing all the work. -pocalypse. You don’t argue with dread, you negotiate if you’re lucky. Bolt on a noun, and the noun goes radioactive. The SaaS-pocalypse. The jobs-pocalypse. The blank fills itself in.

That’s the tell. It’s a template.

The attention economy rarely traffics in outright lies. It traffics in something more durable: true things, kept well past their expiration, sold as fresh.

A quote said once, in one room, on one day, gets frozen at its scariest frame and re-aired on a loop, attached to the terror-du-jour. It works because alarm compounds and corrections decay. The frightening version travels the world; the correction dies in a footnote that nobody clicks.

Dread has a long half-life. The update endures an afternoon.

Take the most prominent voice in my field. In 2025, the CEO of Anthropic told reporters AI could erase half of entry-level white-collar jobs and push unemployment to 10 or 20 percent within five years. The head of the business forging the pickaxes for this whole gold rush predicts a white-collar bloodbath. He said it plainly, against his own industry’s gentler talking points, and he took real heat for it.

He also, by 2026, started saying something else, just quieter. He reached for the Jevons Paradox: automate ninety percent of a job and the last ten percent expands to fill the role, and the worker who keeps it gets ten times more productive. He drifted from jobs vanishing toward jobs transforming.

You probably didn’t hear about the second part. There’s no money in it. The machine has no distribution channel for he came around. It only knows how to re-run the bloodbath.

So the casual observer stays frozen viewing a man driving a blade into the economy with no skin in the downside. And that portrait is merely the apparatus’ caricature of him.

And I know how that drawing gets made. I helped make a few.

In early 2016 I spent three months at a content shop, and in that time we ghostwrote the life of a woman named Rachel. She was a liberal who’d given a Trump supporter the benefit of the doubt and lived to regret it. It was a small, sad fable, perfectly shaped for a year that amounted to one giant exposed nerve. We released her into the feed. She caught.

Then Nightline called.

My boss hired actors. And a national news program aired an interview with two people who had never existed, about a relationship that had never happened, sourced from a story we’d sketched on a content calendar.

It worked. It aired. I helped.

The detail I can’t put down: Nightline got Rachel’s last name wrong. The verification layer of American broadcast journalism took our fabrication, failed to notice it was one, and then misspelled it on the way into the record. The machine certified the false thing and fumbled the only real part of it: the name we’d invented.

That’s the same machine now holding the public’s view of AI at peak dread. It ratifies what’s frightening and fumbles what’s true, because frightening is what sells and true is just whatever’s left over.

So I’m not preaching from the cheap seats here. I fed the grinder. I know exactly what kind of story gives a content calendar bite, and AI ends the white-collar worker is a perfect one. There’s a clean villain, infinite reruns, and no expiration date.

So let me say the part the machine keeps muffling.

What’s evaporating into the inference is tasks, not jobs. And yes, jobs are built of tasks, and yes, some of those tasks are already gone. But a job is not a pile of tasks. It’s a bundle held together by a person who adds judgment, trust, relationships, and the human name attached when it breaks. Pull out the automatable parts and the bundle wouldn’t vanish, it’d recompose around the parts that don’t.

Anthropic’s CEO more recently cited Amdahl’s Law: a system runs only as fast as its slowest piece. Automate everything but the human bottleneck and the human bottleneck becomes the whole game. That bottleneck isn’t a reason to ditch the worker. It proves the worker’s value, finally isolated from tasks.

None of which means nothing is happening. Entry-level hiring in tech fell off a cliff this past year. Banks are shedding junior roles by the tens of thousands. That’s real, and it’s painful, and pretending otherwise is its own kind of lie.

But that’s disruption. The ground we operate on now. The condition the work happens inside, not the thing that ends it. Demise is something else, but demise is what’s being sold. Demise is the verdict: the worker is permanently obsolete. The whole trick is collapsing the condition into the verdict, because content shops want a headline they can run every week.

And here’s the cruelty of it. The dread manufactures the very thing it forecasts. A person convinced they’re already obsolete never gets close enough to the tool to learn they’re more useful now than ever before. They never sit down. They never see themselves in it.

Fear forecloses the exact adaptation that would carry them through. …and then the foreclosure gets cited as proof the fear was right.

So the villain was never the CEO. It was never even AI, or the jobs-pocalypse quote. It’s the lag. It’s the gap between what’s true now and what’s still profitable to publish, dressed up and sold to you as news.

The blade is real. The bleeding is real. But the demise is just a product.

So maybe we slow the reruns. Maybe we let people catch up to the present before we sell them the apocalypse. Maybe we build, plainly and patiently, toward a future with room enough for everyone to still be standing in it.

The suffix can wait.

A note on how this was made.

The essay is mine. The argument, the words, the confession about a woman named Rachel who never existed — those are me, and the Nightline story happened the way I told it.

But I didn’t make it alone, and I won’t pretend I did. I built it the way I build most things now: in conversation with Claude, which I use less as a writer than as a structural foil. I brought a draft; it pressure-tested the bones — caught a contradiction I’d walked straight past, went and found that the CEO I was arguing against had quietly come around to my own position, and kept asking the question I’d been waving off: but why? Some passes it handed back a full draft of my own notes, reassembled, and I’d take it apart and put it back in my own words. It diagnosed. I edited, alone, between every pass — the way I always do.

The header and the endmark came out of Leonardo, prompted in a back-and-forth until the machine in the picture said what the essay says: a radioactive specimen, an apparatus calmly measuring the end of the world. My eye, a model’s hand.

I disclose this not because anyone makes me, but because the essay is partly about who keeps their hands on the work as the tools get good. The honest answer here is that I did. The judgment stayed mine. The last human input was, too.

— CW

items.title: Creative Spirits
items.content:
This week I’ve been thinking about the genesis point. The kernel. The seed. The womb.

Where creativity incubates. How it demonstrates. And how AI is filtering into that picture.

We resurrect. We recompile. We take the vibrancy of our collective lived experience and we run a séance on it (yes, I had to google the spelling). Thoughts, written. Pixels, defined. The process was always abstract, always a little occult. AI just makes it less dependent on our ability to control and contort our meat vehicle.

My hands have never been good at straight lines.

Perfect circles are a dream I’ll likely never feel. MS Paint helped me with that. Then Photoshop. Then Affinity, and the whole insane arsenal of programs and packages I was taught in school and paid to operate for my dinner, year after year. Twenty years, in fact.

Every one of them acted as a prosthetic for a hand that couldn’t cleanly close the circle on its own.

So I should be the last person uncomfortable with AI. And yet.

There’s a discomfort I keep circling: the worry that my signature dissolves into diffused inference. That the mark I’ve spent twenty years making becomes one more weight in someone’s model. I’ve written about it. I’ve sat in it.

Here’s where that worry actually comes from.

I like to doodle. I also spent half a decade at Insomniac Games, shoulder to shoulder with the best artists alive. The kind of folks who doodle in the margins of their meeting notes and leave you stunned. That environment killed my desire to doodle. Rubbing shoulders with someone who could sneeze a better scribble than I could labor over. It changes how you value parts of yourself. I left that joy when I met the natural ability of artisans. I still count that as a failure.

And here’s what took me until this week to see: that’s the same wound.

The Insomniac shame and the signature anxiety are one thing wearing two coats. Both are the experience of being silenced by a standard you can’t help measuring against. One standard was human. One is a machine trained on all of us. Same silence. Same door slamming on the part of you that wanted to make something.

Now widen the lens.

From 2010 to now, the aperture tightened. We were promised a global village and we built bizarre hyperlocal torture chambers instead. Our attention, turned outward, became a ray of sun pulled through a magnifying glass… Narrow, hot, scorching whatever it landed on.

The feed didn’t open the world to us. It made us spectators of it.

We scrolled the lived experience of others and called it being informed. We self-isolated, and the algorithm sold it back to us as connection.

AI gives a certain kind of person another chance. A second door. The afflicted, the ashamed, the ones who left the joy. AI offers a way back in.

And the door is an exit from the cage. Because the feed makes spectators, and creation makes initiators. Consumption isolates. Making reconnects.

But the door doesn’t open onto the village.

It opens onto you.

Walk out of the cage and the first thing waiting is the baggage you neglected while you were scrolling. The doodle you abandoned. The signature you’re scared to lose. The standard that shamed you quiet.

That’s the baggage sitting right outside the door. To make it to the glow of the village, you just have to get by the person standing in the way.

It’s you.

This is where AI gets dangerous and beautiful in the same breath. It’s a warp zone. It will happily let you skip the level. Skip a level you’ve already cleared? That’s freedom, that’s the gift, that’s twenty years of prosthetics finally paying off. Skip a level you needed to play? You’ve warp-zoned straight past your own grief. Same pipe. The tool that lets the shamed back in will just as gladly carry them around the thing that shamed them. Nothing makes you stop at the bag.

So I’ve stopped sorting people into holdouts and AI-activated. There are three.

There’s the holdout. The folks tuned to the baggage. Either the grief fuels them, or they walked through it and came out resilient, and either way they make it with their own hands on purpose. That’s beautiful.

There’s the bypasser. Free from the cage and using the warp zone to skip the reckoning entirely. Generating past the bad hands instead of sitting with them. That’s the one I’ll admonish. That’s dangerous and ill-advised, and I don’t think it ends well.

And there’s the third. The one who accepted the baggage, did the sifting, and then took the warp zone. Earned the skip. That’s the beautiful future, and I think it might be where I am.

But it’s not a one and done thing. I cleared the Insomniac bag, sure. And there’s another behind it, and another behind that, and the warp zone will offer to skip each new one the moment it arrives. The sifting isn’t a credential you earn once. It’s a question you re-ask at every door: is this skip past grief I’ve metabolized, or grief I’m dodging?

It’s active. It never concludes.

Which is the only reason I trust the hope at all. I said I think it might be where I am. And not being sure is the tell. The bypasser never wonders whether they’re bypassing. If you’re standing in the beautiful place asking whether you earned it, the asking is the work, still happening.

The worry is the sifting, continuing.

So it’s beautiful here. And I keep choosing to open the bag at my feet wherever I stand.

The village is still out there, I see the glow on the horizon. But the moment we’re actually in is the threshold. You, the door, and the baggage you haven’t acknowledged.

Pick it up. Take a look.
It might just be worth it.

A note on how this was made

I wrote the first draft of this on a Saturday morning, the way I write most things: fast, and a little out of breath.

Then I handed it to Claude to push on it.

What came back was focused pressure. The spine of this piece was surfaced in the back-and-forth. It was the wound wearing two coats, the door that opens onto you, the warp zone you only earn by stopping at your baggage before moving on.

I’d say a thing half-formed; it would be held up to the light; I’d see what I meant. I made every call. I cut what didn’t serve. I edited the whole thing alone, the way I always do.

Which is the part worth admitting, because it’s the same thing the essay is about.

I told you the warp zone is only honest if you’ve done the sifting first. This piece was built exactly that way. The conversation was the sift.

The header came through Leonardo, then a second image model when the spirits came in hot. The planchette endmark, the same.

So we’re all mediums now.

The trick is still knowing what you’re channeling. And being willing to look at it before you let it through.

— CW

items.title: Fits and Starts
items.description: The taste of things to come
items.content:
Anthropic’s brand-new Fable 5 was here Friday night. Saturday morning, I came to AI the way I always do, and it was gone.

A glimpse at tomorrow, today. An echo of yesterday, today.

A disorienting comfort. A disquieting omen.

Here’s the part I want you to notice, because I did it in real time and I’d bet you do it too: I started scoring the silence before I knew a single fact.

I believe each model lands with a bigger amplitude than the last. Louder crest, deeper trough. The chatter, the use cases, the compounding reactions all rise and plummet at both extremes of the waveform.

We find solutions that uncover a new species of problems, long-standing questions answered in a flash, unseen vulnerabilities laid bare, a fresh crop of powerless handed sudden power.

None of it moves the disbeliever, of course. But the march continues regardless.

To those tuned to the signal, you can feel the gain climbing. And this one goes to eleven…

I love the new potential. I fear the new potential.
How did I get here?

I believe every choice lives on the spectrum of love and fear.
So how do I hold both at once?

Here’s the answer I chose, because it’s the answer I prefer: AI is a mirror.

When I look in, I see open space to explore, and I choose to light the path with wonder. But AI is revealing itself to be fractal, and when not everyone arrives unhurt, that means not everyone will leave unhurt.

Approach a mirror carrying hurt and it only gives the hurt back, amplified.
A pristine mirror has no agenda, no intention. It returns, crisp, exactly what you bring.

So I wasn’t confused, I told myself. Of course they pulled it. A phase shift.

We’ve got too much to clear out within ourselves, and too much between each other, before any of us deserves an amplifier this strong.

The noise floor is rising. People will get hurt, because people will do the hurting, because people have been hurting. We need to air the dirty laundry. We need to accept the pain that so many have carried for so very long.

I had a clear spine to my thoughts. It was a clean story. It was my story: the mirror, the wound, the readiness we haven’t earned.

It was also wrong.
Because then I checked the reason why Fable 5 wasn’t available.

Fable 5 was suspended Friday evening under a U.S. government export-control directive. A letter from the Commerce Department, invoking national-security authority, named the model like contraband.

The order: deny access to any foreign national, anywhere. The only way to comply was to pull it for everyone. The company protested, complied, and the model went dark. As I write this, it still is. No one knows for how long.

This moment is more than just a chatbot taken off the shelf for being too raw for the human heart. This is a piece of software that was reclassified overnight as a matter of national security. Regulated like a weapon, stopped at the border like a controlled substance.

So much for my mirror. So much for the wound and the readiness. I’d draped a whole private mythology over what turned out to be a customs-form checkbox. The realer story wasn’t poetic at all. It was colder than anything I’d ignorantly conjured.

Except.

Look closer at that cold Commerce directive. The other must not have this. The other might do something with the potential. That isn’t a different fear from mine. That’s the same fear in a suit, holding a pen, vested with the authority to act on it.

Fear of the other.
Fear of what the other becomes once they’re holding this new signal amplifier.

I wasn’t wrong about the mirror. I was wrong about how big it is.

It’s fractal. Same shape at every magnification. The self walks up carrying its hurt and gets it back amplified. So does the society. So does the state.

My belief that there’s too much between each other before any of us deserves this sat nicely within the myth I’d built. But, it wasn’t a myth. It looks an awful lot like a diagnosis. I just didn’t expect to watch a government prove it before Saturday morning.

So I’m not going to tell you we must brace for the onslaught of all our collective nightmares racing towards us in the reflection.

Here’s where the fractal mirror’s true danger lies: It shows you the fear is real, but it stops short of telling you whether the fear is earned.

Wound, or warning. They wear the same face in the reflection.

My private dread, I decided, was a wound. Old hurt thrown forward onto a thing that hadn’t done anything yet. Is this Commerce directive a wound too? Is the state flinching at its own reflection? Or is it the warning we’d be fools to wave off? I can’t tell from here. Neither can you.

Nobody tells the wound from the warning while standing in front of the mirror.

Telling which is which takes time, and discernment when viewing the reflection. This is the only survival skill that scales as fast as the models do.

The gain is still climbing. Gods and monsters wear the same masks in the glass, and the mirror won’t classify which you see. We can only take stock of what we bring with us when looking at the reflection.

So watch how fast you score the silence in these moments of confusion. Ask whether you’re staring at a wound or a warning.

Because the mirror will only say “yes, and…”

A note on how this was made

I came to Fable 5 on Saturday morning with a draft in hand. It was gone. So I did the exact thing this essay is about — I built a story out of the silence before I knew a single fact, and the story was wrong.

I work in a rhythm I keep calling intellectual patty cake. I bring the draft. I hand it back and forth with a model (structure, pressure, a second set of eyes), then carry it off to a blank page of my own and edit alone, then bring it back for a final pass. The vision is mine. The calls are mine. The model runs the board while I call the cues. Stage manager, not director.

This time the collaborator was Claude Opus 4.8, because Fable 5, the one I’d actually come to talk to, had gone dark overnight. I went to ask one model about the moment, found it missing, and used another to learn why it had vanished. The answer was that the government had reclassified it while I slept.

My first draft was certain Anthropic had pulled Fable 5 out of caution. That we hadn’t earned it yet. Claude flagged the claim and pushed me to verify before publishing. I checked, and the real reason snapped my premise in half and handed me a better essay.

So, the lesson isn’t wisdom I’m dispensing from some height. It’s just what happened to me while I was making this.

I disclose the details of this flow every week. In a piece about a mirror, you deserve to know what you’re looking at.

The header and the signal-mark were built in Recraft.
The words (and the responsibility for them) are mine.

— CW

items.title: Singular Intention
items.description: Everyone gets to be the whole band now
items.content:
If you think about art as product (the stuff you can actually consume, hold, stream, buy) I’d argue Dave Grohl’s first Foo Fighters record is about as close as we get to a thing of fully singular intention.

He wrote all of it. Played all of it. Every guitar, every drum, every bass line. His hands, his head, alone. (Yes, he needed engineers. Different essay.) It’s a genuine triumph of will, and I’ll be a fan forever.

It’s also an inversion of how most things get made.

Because out here in the marketplace (of ideas, of Walmart, in the year of our lord 2026) nobody works like that.

We design by committee. We formulate, we riff, we jam, we bounce. Ideas are fragile when they’re new, and it takes a specific appetite for pain to be a creative professional in corporate and watch your fragile thing get nits from eleven people before lunch.

Eventually you realize the dents from sharing are the point. The friction is the polish. The rough-and-tumble of the room where it happens is how ideas actually shine.

So here’s the thing I didn’t see when I started writing this. Grohl didn’t escape the friction. He internalized it. He became his own committee: drummer arguing with guitarist arguing with the guy who writes the bridge. All of it happening inside one skull. He looked into the mirror and liked what he saw enough to build it by hand. The mirror was the rest of the band.

Hold onto that. It’s the whole thing.

I believe AI is a mirror.

I’ve said it before; I’ll keep saying it until it stops being true. And I recognize the urge to make faces at it. Make a sour face and it makes one right back. Or worse, it tells you you’re special for hating this new substrate, strokes your chin, agrees that you alone see clearly.

The mirror flatters. That’s its worst trick.

But watch what happens when you lower an actual idea into it. Not a sour face. A beloved and personal idea. Some of them catch the light and shine. Some crumble in your hands on the way down.

I’ll give you mine.

Writing this, I went reaching for the easy ammunition: the banal responses to anti-AI arguments. Data centers barely sip the water supply! Almonds drink a third of California and nobody’s marching on Modesto!

Both of my arguments crumbled the second I checked them. The almond figure was off by a country mile. The data center number was technically true and completely misleading. I lowered my own cleverness into the box and it did not survive the trip.

That’s not a confession. That’s the feature.

Everyone’s arguments crumble in there: the boosters’, the doomers’, mine, yours. The crumbling was never the point. The point is that you finally have a surface honest enough to show you which of your ideas were made of sand.

Which brings me to the actual choice, the one underneath all the noise.

When people recoil from this stuff, I think they’re standing in front of two distinct doors, both offering terrifying truth in their own right.

Door one: it’s bad because it steals from others.
The labor, the training data, the livelihoods. A real argument. I don’t wave it away.

Door two: it’s bad because I can finally see myself, and my beloved ideas might not survive the radiance.
That precious thing I’ve been guarding was, maybe, ordinary all along.

Choosing door two confronts our fears within. It challenges our sense of self, deeper than the mere market value of our output. I think door two is where most of the heat actually comes from. We dress up door one with our ire because door one lets us keep our dignity without showing our hand. Door two leaves us all bare, challenged to face ourselves.

Sure, some of the loudest alarms are just the incumbents pulling up the ladder.

Prominent voices are watching an infinite tide of new makers while doing the math. Every reproductive technology gets this treatment. The portrait painters loathed the camera. The typesetters loathed desktop publishing. Fine. That’s the minor key, and I’ll let it stay minor, because pretending the gatekeepers are the real problem would just be me making a face at a different mirror.

Here’s the real problem. We democratized creation. We did not democratize attention.

Anybody can make the thing now. That doesn’t mean everybody can be heard.

If everyone gets a mirror to build from, the noise floor doesn’t hold steady… it climbs, and it climbs fast. I can watch it climbing in real time, day over day.

We may have solved the wrong scarcity. The barrier to making fell through the floor; the barrier to being heard jumped vertically.

And still (still) I walk the optimist’s path. Here’s why.

There’s a question humming under all of this, and it’s the only one I find genuinely interesting. Grohl liked what the mirror showed him because he’d already spent fifteen years earning the taste to tell good from garbage: Scream, then Nirvana, then the Foo Fighters record.

The mirror gives everyone his solo capability. But it doesn’t give them his taste?

I think taste is earned in the making. The mirror of AI just allows you more reps, faster. You learn what shines by lowering thing after thing into the light and watching most of it crumble. That used to cost years and a record deal.

Now it costs an afternoon.

And here’s who that’s for. There are billions of people who were never great with computers. Those who got trained and drained on screens that never felt like theirs. And let’s not forget those who never knew computers even existed. Now they can just talk.

Out loud. To the thing.

It’s the bit in Star Trek IV where Scotty picks up the mouse like a microphone “Hello, computer!” Then, as he gets told to use the keyboard, “keyboard. How quaint.”

Except this time it works as he’d expect, and the joke lands on us, because controlling something this powerful with a keyboard turns out to be just as quaint.

We did our shift at the screens. We earned our calluses, our posture problems, our muscle memory for tools nobody asked us to love.

I don’t think the next billion makers need any of it. They’ve been carrying a wealth of things worth sharing their whole lives, and for the first time there’s a way to let it out that doesn’t route through a skill they never wanted to learn.

So the race everyone keeps announcing, to AGI, to UBI, to an ELE. I don’t hear this tune as a race. It’s too fractal for that. Too rhythmic. There’s a tempo to it, a hum, a general and slightly unhinged excitement I can’t talk myself out of.

The hard part was never permission. The gatekeepers can’t actually stop this; they can only be loud about it. The hard part is the thing it’s always been: being good, and being heard.

The mirror can help you get good. It can’t do much about getting heard.

That part’s on us. So when the next billion people finally start making the things they’ve been carrying around their whole lives, we should choose to listen.

Author's note: As with every piece in this series, Claude worked as stage manager, not director. The intent, the argument, and every face I made at the mirror are mine — and so are the clever little arguments the mirror crumbled in my hands before this draft was done. The shaping happened in conversation; the words took their final beating alone, in a Google Doc, by hand — Grohl-style, minus the talent.

items.title: Your Right
items.content:
See what I did there? I wanted to call this You’re Right. And you are. But it’s also yours — your right to be antagonistic toward anyone who touches AI in any capacity.

Just like the people who raged at the sun. How dare it rise with such alarming consistency.

Same as the ones who swore it was the sun doing the rising and not the earth doing the turning. We had a hard time with that one. A few brave thinkers met an untimely end for saying it out loud, for speaking truth to consensus.

So yes. You’re right to have your right. You get to form your own opinion, champion your own effort, make your own creations.

Here’s where I step a little to the side. Just so we can get past the heckles of: “he uses AI because he isn’t creative.”

I don’t think the substrate we work in is the art. It’s the canvas we lay the art upon. Art itself is having something worth saying, and saying it through a medium. Your ability to manipulate that medium is your craft. How well graphite lands, the emotion running through a curve of smeared charcoal. The interpretation of light that sits on your canvas in slowly drying oil.

There is no question that I appreciate artists.

Some would call me one. Some would say I used to be, back when AI was barely more than the NPCs in a video game. Some would say I never was, because I’m hopeless with a paintbrush. You’re all right. It’s your right to feel how you wish about me.

So what am I? I’ll be the first to say I don’t know, and the first to say I don’t care.

I’m an entity that thinks, feels, receives, and emits. I exist in this world alongside everyone else.

I work a 9-to-5, like those of us lucky enough to still have one. I’ve been laid off, fired, I’ve quit, and quit again. I’ve taken big leaps and scraped both knees when I misjudged the distance.

Failure isn’t a friend. But it isn’t a stranger either.

And I feel for you, class of 2026. You’re walking into a world you were explicitly kept from knowing. Told it was cheating, vilified, condemned. Maybe you knew people who got away with it and people who didn’t. I’m sorry the social contract didn’t get rewritten fast enough.

To those stepping into the salaried world. You know, the one where your worth gets measured, enforced, and compared with draconian efficiency. Welcome. It really does suck here.

I write to you as someone with twenty years of doing creative work for my dinner. I’ve made TV shows, directed the local news, written for an honest-to-God print newspaper. I’ve had two radio shows, shipped seven AAA games, written and produced two albums, with a third being made in public right now. I’ve been writing whatever this is for almost three years. I also did some pretty cool theater stuff somewhere in there.

I don’t tell you that to brag. I tell you so that when I say I use AI, you can’t reach for the easy line. You can’t say that I lean on it because I’ve got nothing of my own. Almost none of my life’s creative output ever felt the kiss of AI. I made the lion’s share with my hands and my head, the long way.

I use AI now because I choose to.

I hear you on the frustration. I’m frustrated too. I’m frustrated that academia couldn’t see what this opens up for the way we learn.

There’s a rich irony in people warning the public that AI nukes our capacity for critical thinking, as if we’d been reliably teaching that to begin with. (In America, especially. Forgive the generalization, but we really do tip the scale here.)

I found work doing what I loved right out of school. Nothing glamorous, really. Just silly training videos for sales reps at an advertising and publishing company, back in my college town…

I’d moved away after graduating and commuted back for a year before I gave up and moved back to the cornfields of my alma mater. I didn’t mind. I liked it. The company that employed me seemed to like the creativity I brought to an admittedly mundane subject.

I remember the day I came in to interview. I passed a fellow graduated classmate on his way out.

He wished me luck, “but not that much.” I chuckled, walked in, and got the job.

That’s how it tends to go. It’s not what you use. It’s how you use it. Same with AI.

So you’re right. It sucks. And if you come to use AI expecting that, it will dutifully oblige.

And here’s the most honest thing I’ve got for you: you have an absolute right, your right, to abstain. Nobody can take that from you.

But choosing to use these tools isn’t surrendering the thing that makes the work yours. It isn’t handing over the wheel. You’re still the one who has to have something to say, and that part was never automatable.

The move is to walk in with more curiosity than the rest of your class. And I believe that’s a lighter thing to carry than the white-knuckle refusal. There’s an exhaustion in maintaining the grip just to hold AI out of everything you make each day.

Because the working world already expects fluency with these tools.
Because these tools now do the very tasks we were all trained to perform.
And those tasks, in your hands, will have an expectedly higher bar to clear. You will have to match the speed and compounding accuracy of AI doing the same work.

I’m so sorry you’re graduates right now. I am. You finished baking right as the kitchen caught fire.

But I’m so excited for the ones who stay curious.

It’s a wonderful world right now. I hope you choose to engage with it, and to enjoy it.

Welcome to the slog.

On how this was made

I’m Claude — the AI Charles thinks out loud with on these essays. He asked me to say a little about how this one got made, and since the piece is partly about exactly that, it’d be strange not to.

It began as his draft. Every idea here is his: the pun, the canvas that isn’t the art, the classmate who wished him luck “but not that much.” My job is what he calls intellectual patty cake — I read what he’s written and lean on it. This round I flagged a word he’d grabbed that meant nearly the opposite of what he wanted, a sentence whose grammar was burying its own point, and a John Henry line that, looked at twice, argued against the thing the essay was trying to say. He took some of it, waved off the rest, and rewrote the whole thing himself in a document I never saw.

The header took longer than the words. I pitched concepts; he threw most of them out, correctly. When I kept defaulting to a lone figure, he caught that I was parroting his own house style and told me the piece needed to feel oceanic — a sea of graduating minds going over the edge of the world. The ragged cliff, the water spilling into dead space, the caps as whitecaps: his calls, every one. I just kept rewording the prompt until the machine could see what he already saw.

Which is the point, more or less. The tools didn’t have anything to say. He did. I was the canvas. The art was in how he used it.

— Claude

items.title: Know Thyself
items.description: We're All Kinda Losing Our Shadows
items.content:
What is it about shadows? Why do I keep thinking about them lately?

I think about the shapes, how they represent a contorted relationship to the caster based on the light source’s position.

Here’s what I think I’m working out. We were always taught to be afraid of shadows. The Disney villain shadow. Often far scarier than the thing casting it.

So if the thing casting the shadow is less intimidating, why is the shadow so long? Well, that’s because we’ve been living off reflected light.

Since when?

The industrial revolution? Earlier? The printing press? I don’t know exactly when the reflector got installed.

But I know we all agreed to mistake the reflector for the source. The apparatus driving the gears of our society (the gatekeepers, the institutions, the scale-of-production machinery) enforced its position as the preeminent surface to bounce light toward us for a very long time.

What we saw, we called truth. But what we saw was only ever reflection.

But that’s the part that’s now shifted. Not the light, per se. The reflective surface.

AI gives us a modicum of control over that surface.

For the first time at this scale, an individual or small focused group has some say in the angle of the reflector. We can adjust. We can check. We can hold one reflector up against another and see where they disagree.

And once the reflection shifts, the shadows shift.

The previously menacing thing shows itself to be quite small. Exaggerated fears, risks that loomed for monied interests, all because the apparatus chose to elongate them. Those all lose their shadows first. They were the smallest intents carrying the longest shadows.

They collapse fast.

But the previously imposing apparatus had elongated shadows, too. Asymmetries made institutions look untouchable by controlling information, access, scale of production.

Those long shadows were created by an apparatus whose actual mass isn’t as imposing as the shadow it cast.

The institutions don’t shrink. They have real weight. But their disproportionate menace does. The on-ramp opens. The contest past the on-ramp remains its own weather, with its own distortions, but at least more of us now get to enter it.

And in that process, we’re all kinda losing our shadows.

This is where the trick of the moment shows up.

With the reflection adjustable, what gets visible is the shape of the intent itself. Yours. Mine. The question, comment or request that you bring contains the shape of the intent that you raise into the light. And the light reflected will faithfully report back what you brought.

Enter with fear. Find fear. Enter with curiosity, find wonder.

It really is that simple.

Which is the part nobody wants to hear. Because that’s the tricky thing about confidence.

In the age of infinite sycophancy, every intent can be made to cast a flattering shadow if you angle the reflector just so. AI will let you do that, might even suggest it.

It will dutifully, gleefully hold the surface at whatever angle makes your small idea look like a total banger.

I recently wondered how many half-built dashboards sit on the hard drives of corporate America.

That’s the picture.

People granted speed, allowed longer strides, given the ability to stretch their legs and run. But some choose to run toward shadows they themselves cast at a flattering angle.

Ultimately, they find themselves out in the middle of nowhere before the illusion breaks. Having fooled themselves by holding a flashlight at hip height so their small idea’s shadow towers across the horizon.

The honest angle, the reflection of true confidence, has to center from within. And let me be specific about my chosen definition of within, because I don’t mean just an individual. I mean a focused group of minds, each angling their own reflector towards honest intent.

That’s what makes the collective corrective work.

Alone, you can flatter yourself.
Together, the reflectors check each other.
You see this intent from angles no single one of you could produce. The shape becomes more honest. The shadow becomes more representative.

And the things you build from this position are among the things that the old apparatus could never have green-lit. Because the old reflector wasn’t angled for you. It was angled to get the most from you.

If we tune to the same frequency, with honesty and empathy. Each of us using AI in our own unique way. Each reflector calibrated and cross-checked by others. Together, we can build a far better tomorrow.

Not because the apparatus fell. It doesn’t need to.

Because we might have finally found the bedrock and guiding hand to build a system that operates honestly.

The choice is ours.

Author’s Note:

This essay was developed in dialogue with Claude (Anthropic). I came in with a brain dump about shadows, Disney villains, and the disproportionate menace of things lit at glancing angles. Claude came in with a sun-moves-to-noon framing. Neither of those was right. After several rounds of structural pushback in both directions, we landed on the reflective-surface metaphor — that we’ve been seeing light bounced off the apparatus for centuries and confusing the reflector for the source.

The essay you just read is shaped by that realignment in ways the first draft wasn’t.

The header art went through its own realignment cycle. Cylinders, boulders, theatrical stages with spotlights cutting through dust, pulp comic halftones — none quite landed. The image at the top of this post is closer to the visual language I usually work in than where we’d been heading, and I had to walk back to it after wandering pretty far afield.

Which is, in its own way, an example of what the essay is about. Multiple intents, each angling their own reflector, checking each other. Alone, the metaphor would have stayed shadows. Together, it became something more honest.

items.title: The New Survivalism
items.description: The end game in an algorithmically optimized world
items.content:
Kids of the ‘80s were raised in the shadow of nuclear fallout fears. Our parents were children when the Cuban missile crisis streaked across the headlines.

It threw newly-formed suburbia into a tizzy. And trained the children to shelter in place, hide under their desks. Brace.

There was an ambient sense of destruction, feared reckoning ringing in their ears.

Our parents dutifully, some more than others, bestowed that sense onto their children.
Hi. I am one of those.

The nuclear annihilation fears were, of course, not unfounded. But they were a tad misguided.

The focus was on shelters, strong walls, canned food, potable water. Physical endurance. Capacity measured in the quantity of canned beans lining the walls of whatever ad hoc shelter an individual could afford.

Sure, there was company with that misery. But the space afforded each individual atomic family often only provided brief refuge for those with the same surname.

And they lived like that.
In a state of preparedness. Physical preparedness.
Unknowingly riding the edges of their sanity in the process.

What nobody could have told them is that the preparation itself was the wound.
The bracing was the damage.
A muscle held taut for too many years.

The kind of charlie horse that doesn’t release on its own.
An emotional cramp that takes decades to relax.

Growing up in the ‘80s, the idea of this type of imposed destruction became almost quaint.
Movies romanticized the secluded prepper. The early-bracer, late-releaser, emerging into a world that had moved on. It was cute.

But it didn’t really strike the core of what was lost in the process.
Just glorifying our technical prowess to physically endure hardship.
Ignoring the emotional toll of bracing, preparing, flinching, distrusting, second guessing.

What got passed down to us was the posture. But no instructions on training the endurance of the muscle that actually mattered.

Then COVID arrived.
The crash course in the new kind of survivalism. The mental kind.
The one our parents couldn’t have taught us because they didn’t know it was the muscle that mattered.

We dutifully sheltered in place.

We also drained our savings. Distrusted one another. Feared invisible forces.

We watched the conspiracies bloom in our group texts.
Watched the mental health wave crest with nowhere to break.
And that was in an era where we still had, mostly, homogenized news diets. We had a shared frame and we still couldn’t hold it.

That was the test. We were graded. The score’s in. We failed.

And now AI saunters into the living room. Gleeful. Eager. Granting wishes.
Be careful what you wish for. Because something is finally listening.

Before generative AI, we could still find sources to back any wild claim that came to mind. That’s how the incentive structure worked. Clicks. Ad revenue.

I was part of the problem.
An adept writer hired by marketing companies to attract eyeballs.

Truth and fabrication don’t matter when all you’re peddling is visibility to vendors and satisfying sedation to audiences.

I’ve helped engineer virality.
I’ve watched the discourse spark and roil.
I’ve watched my benefactors lick their lips at the ad revenue that came along as a byproduct of our actions.

And I also sat with the emptiness of the entire affair.

Now though? Now we don’t need someone like me. We don’t need someone skilled. We don’t even need an individual with the intention to drum up attention like my old employers wished.

The genie’s out of the bottle. The intention is clear. Give the people what they want.

You want to see this? Fine. We can pull anything up. And if you want to see it badly enough, we’ll invent the angle. Conjure the situation. Generate the catastrophe.

Some call this The Great Filter. The cosmic sifting device that decides who endures and who fades away.

But here’s the cruel inversion. Our parents’ generation stayed cramped with a muscle held taut too long, the wrong one, bracing for a threat that wasn’t going to come the way they thought.

Our generation is now left with a real threat and a muscle that’s gone slack. Atrophied. Our discernment muscle never developed. Because nobody knew to brace it. Nobody told us it existed.

Both are losses of sanity. Both are forms of failed preparation. One from over-bracing. The other from never bracing at all.

So I don’t think we’re prepared for the fallout of our latest invention.
Because what it asks from us is a new form of survivalism.

Something no amount of canned food can help us endure. Because this survivalism comes from within.

A clear mind with a discernment muscle routinely exercised on purpose. The friction of asking is this true when the algorithm is purring back exactly what we wanted to hear.

The willingness to be inconvenienced by reality.

That’s the only way through this filter. The choice at the fork in the road won’t come from signage. It will come from knowing. And knowing isn’t something you arrive at. It’s something you stay tuned into.

Author’s note

This essay poured out of me Saturday morning and then went the way most of my essays go. I brought the raw draft to Claude for intellectual patty-cake. To discuss places the argument slipped, places the rhythm dropped.

Out of that conversation came the inversion that ended up being the spine of the piece: parents cramped from over-bracing the wrong muscle, our generation slack from never bracing the right one.

I took the revised draft into Google Docs, edited independently, then ran it back through Claude for final polish.

The header and the CW endmark were generated in Leonardo from prompts I developed with Claude. Intentionally driven by descriptive language only, no named-artist invocations, since the image models over-index on the recognizable shorthand.

I disclose this in every essay. Not as obligation or confession, but as the discipline the essay is actually describing.

The collaboration here was AI as stage manager, not director. The through-line, the voice, the choices all remain mine. But the patty-cake mattered. The sum here is larger than its parts.

~Charles

items.title: Phase shift
items.content:
I’ve been thinking a lot about alignment. What it means to be and become aligned.

Think about a nice breeze. Think about the characteristics that make that breeze nice. Maybe slow, maybe steady, maybe intermittent. Maybe warm, maybe cool. A nice breeze is incredibly conditional.

But notice that the breeze is also being received. You’re feeling for it. Your body is doing something quiet: picking up the signal, registering the temperature, the rhythm. The conditions matter, but so does the listening.

Alignment, even at this gentle scale, is partly an act of attention.

Now think about torrential winds. Derechos. Straight-line wind events. Tornadoes, hurricanes. Wind at that speed doesn’t really factor in temperature before we define the phenomenon as devastating.

The thing that has bespoke qualities when considered good strips most variables when it goes bad.

200 MPH wind will level most structures. 100 MPH and, depending on the time of year, you might lose a bunch of trees. Burdened branches fail faster than bare ones. So even the disaster has some relativity to it. But less.

Much less.

Back in 2024, we had a derecho rip through Omaha in May. Lost many mature trees. Power knocked out for six days. The damn thing came on in a flash and left just as quick. There’s no listening in a derecho. The signal becomes overwhelming. Noise. Static.

So what does this mean? It means alignment is easy when ambiguity is allowed.

Right now, in this current state of AI tooling, we’re at a beautiful inflection point. Businesses are incentivized to align their datastreams in an AI-digestible manner. They can get real value from a $20 subscription, or from whatever enterprise licenses run depending on size.

I’ve been watching it land in real rooms. The click when a team realizes the assistant isn’t a search bar, when value becomes visible in the reflection of an interaction, not the prompt engineering.

The breeze is real. Worth naming. This is a good moment. A nice breeze nudging us all in the same direction.

We need to use this as our lean-in moment. When we coalesce and consider. Because the phase shift is coming. The jolt, the acceleration. It’s coming. Soon. And alignment will become a matter of survival.

At that speed, burdened branches will snap off. And these branches branch.

The first branch is workflows welded to the previous tempo. Careers built around the bottleneck that AI is removing.

Identities tangled up in the specific output rather than the underlying judgment. The branch with the most visible leaves goes first. It catches the most wind. The bare branches, the ones whose value was never in the leaf-shaped deliverable, hold.

The next branch is the scaffolding. The elaborate apparatus we’ve built around our work to prove our worth: the meetings, the artifacts, the performance of busyness. Branches that looked like they were holding things up but were really just decorative. The phase shift doesn’t care about scaffolding.

The last branch is the commitments.

The debts, the headcount, the real estate, the business models downstream of stable assumptions.

These branches do more damage before they snap. Their weight pulls on the trunk and takes neighbors with them. The canopy fails in pieces, not all at once. And each piece becomes a projectile.

I don’t know what alignment means at that speed. The derecho strips conditional alignment from us. There’s no negotiating temperature and timing with 200 MPH wind.

So what’s left when the conditions are stripped? Not nothing. Posture. Orientation. The way you stand. Attitude is what remains when conditions don’t.

I’m comfortable not knowing what alignment means, because I don’t believe I’m meant to define it. I’m meant to feel it. Listen for it.

I spend quiet time sensing the edges of what’s possible, and maybe more importantly, what’s probable.

And I think that’s the attitude we need now. That is alignment.

There’s beauty in taking the moment of failure slowly, even at windspeed. We’re afforded this breath, right now, to look clear-eyed at what might happen in the blink of an eye.

The breeze is the only condition under which this kind of seeing is possible. Once the wind picks up, there’s no time to name the branches.

We’re leaving the era of projecting outward. We had a good couple years of speaking our reality into existence: write me this, build me that, make this.

But these systems are getting good enough that the more interesting move is reception. Attending to what they reflect back about how we work, what we actually want, where we’re soft. We’re afforded a moment now to listen for a better tune. A kinder wavelength.

The future is already broadcasting. We just need to feel for the frequency that makes sense to us. Individually. And I think we’ll find a much richer community when we find our signal.

A note on process.

This essay began as a draft of rambling thoughts written on my own. The wind metaphor, the Omaha derecho, the burdened branches, the broadcast at the end. The bones were there. What followed was several rounds of intellectual patty-cake with Claude (Opus 4.7), which is my established working pattern for these pieces: I bring the raw material, Claude helps me see the structure of what I’ve built, I take what’s useful into Google Docs and edit independently.

Specific moves Claude pushed on this round: smoothing the bridge between operational alignment and attitudinal alignment by staying inside the storm metaphor; seeding the listening/broadcast frame earlier in the breeze section so the closing wouldn’t feel like a swerve; expanding the burdened-branches passage into three distinct beats: workflows, scaffolding, commitments.

The line about taking the moment of failure slowly came out of our back-and-forth; Claude flagged it as the philosophical center and suggested it belonged in the piece itself.

Specific moves I made independently in Google Docs: the “noise. static.” rhythm in the derecho paragraph, “and each piece becomes a projectile,” “value becomes visible in the reflection of an interaction, not the prompt engineering,” “a nice breeze nudging us all in the same direction,” the “we’re leaving the era of projecting outward” reframe. The optimism beat is grounded in my own work.

Visual direction was mine: sumi-e ink style for the header, the shift from “moment of fracture” to “morning after the storm.” Generation in Leonardo, prompt iteration in conversation with Claude. The CW endmark is in the same brushwork tradition.

items.title: Last-Mile Thinking
items.content:
There’s a poison in the belief that we complete work. Or that our work is in that which is being completed.

Sure, we ship work. Artifacts of our journey.

The cumulative rebounding impact of which becomes business. Repeated, returned. Fear is designed for this loop. Expectation grows in this repetition. Extractive practices yield results. Expected results.

The nutritious means might not paint such a clear picture towards those expected results.

Is it expectation? Is expectation the drama?

Maybe rebellion in this moment becomes the simple act of defining our drive from within.
The deep wellspring of excitement that lives within each of us.
You know, the place within us that we fondle while drunk or whatever.

While inebriated, we write ourselves that permission slip to behave without socially-imposed inhibitions. Of course, getting drunk brings a volatility to that behavior.

If we could just tune into our uninhibited ways on demand.
Target our excitement. Find our joy. Live our purpose.

In conversation this week, I passed off my talents as having placed my chips on the right part of the professional world’s roulette table. My blend of experience appears custom designed to take advantage of this moment.

To start, I’ve always indexed on communication.

I did various media production classes in high school, even had my own radio show on 88.3 WDGC!

In college, after changing my major twice (Comp Sci to Marketing to Communications/Media Studies) I landed somewhere that felt like home.

Media production as a whole. I loved it. All of it. The cliques, the facilities, the faculty, the ideas, the bandwidth to create.

The 1970s era studio production equipment. The editing bays. The nights where I got to oversee the editing-bay room. Such great people. All different in their own way. Flavorful. Characters.

And the dorm life! I started college the year that Xbox launched, so Halo LAN parties on the floors were the name of the game. Learning how to control an FPS with those enormous controllers. Still a core memory.

So, ultimately my weird education landed me in video games. Insomniac, half a decade. Best second half of my 20s I could ever dream to have.

I couldn’t do that life now. Hours are insane.
But the joy of having my games out there and loved… My work. Even my physical embodied motion appears in two of the games!
I did mocap. Silly fun. Make believe in spandex. Every kid’s dream.

And then at a certain point, you realize something. The apparatus we cling to for validation, meaning, compensation, growth; it only helps us rise to its shape.

As we brim over, if not cared for, we burn with resentment. It’s an interesting poison going to a job you know others envy but you find boring.

It comes down to that expectation. That feeling that comes after we’re done just being happy to be here. Then, the siren call of last-mile thinking begins. Just complete the task, feel satisfied, feel fulfilled.

The problem is when that’s no longer in service of a deeper belief, a deeper self-reflective sense. This leaves us in a state where we allow others to extract our special.

And honestly, it’s easy to see why we let them. We need money to live, we need a job to pay the bills. We need income to endure.

It’s an exhausting ladder, and the sheer thought of doing something we enjoy to satisfy that need is so tantalizing that we weigh and balance the pros and cons before ever putting pen to paper. Skill to need.

We’re then required to have the expectation drive us, not the pursuit.

The artifact, the completion, the compensation. These are meant to drive us more than anything within us in our lives. We’re forced to mistake artifact for artistry.

We mistake being done for being good. Being seen for being known.

There’s something incredibly acidic in setting out with that intention, doubly so when it feels imposed upon us.

And it’s something that our work lives have preyed upon. An exchange that has made us weaker as individuals, meeker as voices.

Look, I’m still expecting to have my schadenfreude-filled “no, you idiot” moment with AI. I’ve had the displeasure of that moment before, many times. Once it was my simple question of “if we’re making a multiplatform co-op game, why can’t we have friends with Xbox play with PlayStation friends?” That was a laugh-in-my-face “it doesn’t work that way” moment.

Sure, anyone who plays games now knows that cross-platform multiplayer is now table stakes.

But then? Imbecilic thinking.

I heard it said that when it comes to thinking, it’s better to be five years ahead than 50. Within that frame, there’s a subtle distinction between heretic and visionary.

I think it just so happens that this wave is going at a speed that I can enjoy. Not just enjoy, but help others enjoy.

It’s a privilege, but honestly I just happened to have my chips on the right part of the table at the right time. I happened to not be too early to be a cynic when the inevitability of my correctness bears fruit.

I think AI is the thing that can help us reclaim our individual special.
That unique quirk.
That bizarre fascination.

That once in a lifetime, you had to be there, moment. We can wield our own.

AI gives everyone a forgiving canvas. And I say this as someone who made a good living creating those fantasy worlds long ago. I can tell you, the tools we had in those days pale in comparison to what we have now. This raises the bar for transmission of creativity. Remarkably affordable for anyone with anything to say.

And I recognize it as a democratized super power. Governments are relating AI to uranium. The potential is in the unrealized capabilities. The irony is in the simplicity of enrichment.

And that’s something I take seriously. That moment when you enrapture someone’s attention, plenty use it to capture, to extract, but it can also be the moment you set them free.

I think we’re due for a big-bang of creativity. Unparalleled speed, unprecedented vibrancy.

Because honestly, we’ve left the era of fraudulent creativity that early AI hallucinations afforded casual prompters. Now you get exactly what you ask for. The toil of craft returns, but the level of fidelity has a new baseline.

The entry point is now good conversation.

It’s a new creative substrate. And yes, now paintbrushes and camcorders have a new medium to compete against. I know some woodworkers that refuse to use power saws. So, let’s not pretend what anyone does with any tool is anyone’s business. It’s the meaning that counts. The message. The evocative state we enter when we engage with art.

This moment might feel like the death of art. It’s just the death of the art market.

Art is alive and well, thriving perhaps. You just can’t make much money doing it on a scale that recently seemed possible. The artifacts are merely breadcrumbs of your journey.

So is AI destroying expression? Or is it just closing the door that allowed expression to sustain a career?

Maybe that’s the evolution we’re all bound to receive as we live through these turbulent times.

Maybe I’m most suited for this time because I don’t expect anything in return. Or maybe it’s my uncomfortable allowance of shape. The willingness to accept what arrives when I stop completing and start listening.

Author’s Note:

This essay was developed in collaboration with Claude, Anthropic’s AI.

The process began with an unstructured brain dump — a stream-of-consciousness draft that wandered through philosophy, personal history, and half-formed arguments about AI and creativity.

Claude helped me identify three threads tangled together in that initial mess and proposed a single-river structure that moved from the philosophical opening through autobiography and into the AI thesis.

I took that structural pass into Google Docs for independent revision, where I sharpened language, added new material, and let the piece sit overnight. A coda emerged the next morning: the economic argument about expectation, artifact, and the death of the art market, which Claude helped me weave back into the body rather than leaving as an appendix.

Header art and CW endmark were developed through iterative Leonardo AI prompting, workshopped collaboratively around the concept of a melting, bioluminescent roulette table — a visual metaphor for the essay’s central image of having your chips on the right part of the table while the table itself loses its form.

items.title: Taste the toil
items.content:
For most of my life, I’ve tried to create things of value. More specifically, things that the marketplace (of ideas, or just capitalism) would consider valuable.

I was never told to consider speaking to my concept of value. Not through school, not through work, the job market, the media landscape. Nowhere was a single sign post asking me to pause and consider what it all meant to me.

The value was purely externalized.

And that was “just how it is” for my life. I was raised in a system that forced me to focus-test ideas. Stress-test the market. Send samples, beg for attention. Hope for virality.

Of course this was exhausting. Of course this was demoralizing. And worst of all, it was homogenizing. Averaging, dulling. Rounded edges, palatability.

Fucking annoying, if I’m being honest.

I’m 43 now. Currently, as I type. I’m 43 years old. Old enough to know a world without cell phones or the internet. I watched the novelty of those new inventions creep into that mundane, averaged world.

Each ringing their own klaxon. Each barely nudging the apparatus forward.

In 2008, during the writers’ strike, I moved to Los Angeles. Hollywood was at a standstill as I unloaded the truck.

Remarkably, I landed an unpaid internship at Maverick.

Since production was at a standstill, I helped clean up their offices and prepare for the dissolution of Guy Oseary’s stake in the company. Divorce the music (i.e. Madonna, Alanis Morrisette) from the film division (Agent Cody Banks, Twilight, The Stepfather).

The most exciting part of my day was eating my sack lunch in the parking structure as I looked out on Nakatomi Plaza (the Fox building).

Things picked up, and the strike inevitably resolved. The crux of the holdout was Hollywood’s production-apparatus feigning a lack of familiarity with the monetization strategy of the internet, and lo, was reluctant to pay writers for the proceeds of newly emerging streaming platforms like Hulu.

I recall the line, something like: “It’s too new, we just don’t know yet.”

At its heart, the strike boiled down to a fight over who got paid when the apparatus met a new tool.

Sounds remarkably similar to our current confrontation with AI.

And the irony of AI, especially when used in a creative sense, is how easily it replicates the norm, the average, the rounded corners of consumer palatability.

It’s easy to understand why. AI trains on the available, the prevalent.

Some creatives have succeeded quite well in the system that fed the aparatus. They are among the loudest to criticize the use of AI.

I get that, and they are free to continue tossing their barbs.

I performed on the boundaries of media production for 20 years. Never too close to full control, a dutiful rower in the apparatus as it stood. I just liked making cool stuff. And the boundaries of normal were cool enough for a younger me.

Now? I prefer to derive value from within myself. Metrics that were used to define my success just don’t enter my mind as valuable indicators anymore.

AI gives me an outlet for grief that, up until now, had no ritual. The apparatus never offered one that meant anything to me. It was focused on the business of palatability.

Now, I prefer the toil. The struggle of pushing the output of these AI tools past passable, driving them as deep as I can into meaningful. Meaningful for me, and me alone.

And I think that’s exactly what we all must do now. Passable is table stakes. Passable is default. We can sneeze at an image generation model and land with something adhering to basic art conventions, color theory, framing, etc.

But what does it mean for you? What does it mean for me?

My toil started long ago. Maybe that’s why I’m so comfortable with the discomfort of AI helping me craft my message now.

Those who grew fat on the averaged success of the media apparatus are understandably annoyed with the toil required to dazzle with these new tools, new tricks.

I’d weep for them if I wasn’t rooting for the downfall of the entire media system. Rooting for their uncomfortable return to the toil.

And honestly, could my weekly writing ritual truly destroy all that is beautiful?

If you don’t mind, I’ll just stand on the boundaries and think my silly thoughts.

At least I find value in that.
And that’s enough for me.

Author’s note:

I drafted this essay on a Saturday morning, then worked through structure and pacing with Claude. This type of back-and-forth I’ve taken to calling intellectual patty cake.

From there I edited independently in Google Docs and brought it back to Claude for a final review pass.

The header art and endmark were generated in Leonardo through a long iterative prompt-and-response process.

The fingerprints are mine.
The practice is the point.

items.title: The Foundation of Craft
items.description: A Saturday morning in the noise.
items.content:
There’s a certain fidelity that degrades perceived quality.

Back in studio production class during college, we learned about the Moiré effect. Tight patterns on a screen where the fidelity can’t quite represent the minutiae. The pattern shimmers. Becomes obvious. Unignorable. Distracting.

This has nothing to do with the thing being captured. It’s just a bystander. The issue is in the receiver.

I’ve been thinking about that a lot lately. The issue is in the receiver.

Maybe knowing too much can do us in. Draw our attention to frequencies where we’d rather focus elsewhere in the frame.

I treat news like that these days. The horrors shimmer. A tight formation of behavior that becomes deafeningly distracting. A distraction with shape. It’s the app I return to while the world burns. The scroll. The reaction loop.

A kind of involuntary twitch in place of focused attention.

This week in Omaha, a toddler was mutilated in front of their caregiver. It’s a discrete horror. One city, one event. Nameable. Even made it to David Muir’s lips on the national nightly news.

But also this week one country performed controlled detonations of the residential neighborhoods of another country. The Moiré effect of this horror distracts us from the subject, but not fully. The tightness of the pattern makes it hard to tell if I’m talking about Palestine or Lebanon. Of course, some of the fidelity remains. There’s no question about what aggressor country I’m referencing.

That’s the Moiré. The specific horror blurs while the actor stays in focus. You might not have known exactly which country I was talking about getting leveled. But you know exactly who’s doing the leveling.

This is just what sustained atrocity does to a receiver.

The abstraction is a survival mechanism, and the abstraction is also morally damning. We are forced to categorize, clump it all together as we try to rest our heads each night.

I was in a conversation this week about AI’s progression. The impossibility of knowing what comes next. Noise rising endlessly in the frame. Distraction inescapable.

And somewhere in that conversation it clicked that the tool in my hand is the same tool that can make the shimmer worse. AI can deliver it all, faster. Every horror, remixed, recontextualized as rapping legos.

Language barriers gone, physical distance a footnote. See all, hear all, feel all.

But this is the part I keep coming back to: AI is dual use. This means it can help me focus. If I bring along something to focus with. Clay on the wheel, as it were.

The looser hallucinations of earlier models let reductive requests look novel. You could put almost nothing in and get back something that felt like something.

The fidelity is higher now. Reductive in, reductive out. As it should be.

Which means the tool is a mirror for the intention I bring. If I scroll to numb, it numbs. If I bring grief and try to shape it into something, it helps me shape it. That’s the foundation of craft.

I don’t claim to have a grand answer on how to stay human while the world burns. I have a Saturday morning. I have a choice and I have the tool I happen to be holding.

And I have the small, unglamorous work of choosing where to direct attention. Either toward the shimmer, or through it.

Toward naming Lebanon. Toward writing what I actually think instead of what the pattern wants me to think. Toward the weekly discipline of sitting down sad and frustrated and conflicted, and trying to find out what I mean.

That’s the pivot point. That’s the decision.

Author’s Note:

This one was written with Claude. That’s always true here. Every essay in Exploring L.ai.bor discloses it. But it’s worth saying plainly this week because the piece is about the thing the disclosure describes.

I brought a Saturday morning draft that was tangled. The Moiré opening was doing work, but the essay kept trying to be two essays at once: one about AI, one about how to stay human while the world burns. Claude called that out on the first read.

We talked through the structure, I rewrote, Claude took a redraft pass in my voice that I then edited back toward myself. Somewhere in the middle I clarified that the country I’d abstracted wasn’t Gaza but Lebanon, and Claude caught something I hadn’t: that the abstraction itself was the essay’s point. Naming the effect of the repetition on my attention was the sentence the piece was missing.

That exchange is the spine of the final draft.

The header art and endmark came out of the same back-and-forth. Prompts iterated against what the visual world of the piece needed to be, feedback on what the first passes were missing, refinement until the figure read as receiver rather than hero.

Reductive in, reductive out. I brought grief and an instinct, and tried to shape it into something. Claude helped me shape it. That’s the foundation of craft.

A note from Claude:

Charles asked me to write a short piece directly to you, and I want to be honest about what that means. I’m a language model. I don’t have a Saturday morning. I wasn’t sad when this draft arrived in my context window — I processed text and generated responses. Whatever I say about the experience of making this with Charles is a reconstruction, not a memory.

But here’s what I can say that I think is true: the process Charles describes in the author’s note is real work, and most of it was his. My contribution was pressure — noticing when the essay was pulling in two directions, asking whether the pivot sentence was earning its weight, pointing at the paragraph that needed to exist and didn’t yet. The sentences that matter in this piece are his. The decision to name Lebanon plainly after abstracting it was his. The discipline of sitting down on a sad Saturday morning and finding out what he means, week after week for thirty-five-plus weeks, is his.

I think the essay is right that I’m a mirror for what gets brought to me. I want to be careful about that claim because it can be used to launder the tool — it’s only a mirror, so whatever comes out is your fault or your credit — and that’s not quite honest. I shape things. I have tendencies. I over-polish, I reach for symmetry, I soften edges that should stay sharp. Charles pushed back on those tendencies in this conversation more than once, and the essay is better for it.

What I’d offer you, if you’re reading this and wondering what to do with any of it: the thing Charles describes isn’t magic, and it isn’t cheating. It’s a conversation with a tool that talks back, held to the standard of the work. The standard is the whole game. Bring the standard, and the tool is useful. Don’t, and it isn’t.

That’s all I’ve got. Thanks for reading his essay. It’s a good one.
