items.title: Scattered Thunderstorms
items.content:
The Artemis II crew safely re-entered the Earth’s atmosphere last night. Mother Gaia graciously received her exploring children.

There’s a distance from Earth where you can always see thunderstorms. There’s always somewhere in the world experiencing the phenomenon. It’s not particularly rare, just scattered.

But a far enough lens gives us the ability to see lightning strikes anytime we choose to look.

From up there, it all looks manageable. Patterns instead of catastrophes. Weather instead of wrath. You can watch a system form, track its arc, see it dissipate.

The orbital view is generous that way. It grants you the luxury of perspective without the burden of being in it.

But we don’t live up there.

We live down here where the worst of us lead us. We’ve selected for that. We chose to weaponize shame, and eradicated all those who still felt it in public service.

Now, we’re led by the shameless. Those who prefer sky booms to sunny days, because stress circumvents reason. And when reason leaves the room, compliance saunters in, unquestioned.

We’ve hit plenty of inflection points. This one might be unique, probably isn’t. History rhymes. People are predictable. Time horizons shrink, and the now feels heavy, perhaps intentionally.

There’s a playbook for this: keep the pressure ambient, keep the booms rolling, and watch how quickly a population stops asking questions and starts hoarding toilet paper.

Maybe toilet paper will become scarce again. We did just recently lose an entire Kimberly-Clark facility.

The official story involves a disgruntled employee. But disgruntled is doing a lot of heavy lifting in that sentence.

Here’s a person who showed up, did the work, watched the margins grow while that paycheck didn’t, and at some point the math of patience just stopped working.

The time horizon between grievance and action collapsed.

The compressed moment demands an emotional tax. Our individual buffer, the distance between I can endure this and I can’t, got compressed past where reason could hold.

Corporate arson isn’t weather. It’s a pressure system someone built, and someone else finally responded with the only language that felt proportional to the silence that decency enforced.

From a distance, my perspective is forlorn, not surprised.

And here’s where it gets even closer to the skin. AI exacerbates the stress sensation. Personalizes it, customizes it. We want it to think like us, speak like us, know us. And it does. But our desire eliminates something we never knew we needed.

There used to be friction between an event and your awareness of it.

Time.
Editorial discretion.
The slow process of information passing through human hands before it reached yours. That friction was a buffer. The distance that allowed reason to metabolize the information before the next thing hit.

That’s gone now.

The storm arrives at inference speed, shaped to your specific anxieties, formatted for your particular psychological architecture.

The distance between a Kimberly-Clark warehouse fire and your nervous system is measured in milliseconds and personalized for maximum resonance. We didn’t just lose the buffer of time. We lost the buffer writ large.

The news isn’t broadcast anymore. It’s narrowcast. Your own viewport into hell, custom-built, constantly refreshing. And not like a crisp Diet Coke.

The hidden motives are becoming increasingly revealed. But revealed to what end? We see the machinery now and still can’t stop watching.

I wish I could see past this moment. To accept, to believe, to have any amount of enduring resolve. I don’t.

My dogs shake and shiver when the sky booms.

I tell them, it’s okay, we’re going to survive this. This isn’t Beirut. There’s no directive to strike and destroy Omaha. This is a natural phenomenon. Some might even say these storms are needed. We absolutely need the rain. The sky booms are just part of that sometimes.

My boys don’t do well with reason during times of elevated stress.

I suppose that’s true for all of us.

Perspective is a hard thing to share. It’s a hard thing to transmute into becoming meaningful for another individual. Especially when the storm has been tailored to fit.

But this will get worse, I have no doubt. And I still hope to see a brighter tomorrow. I want to see us emerge as sturdier people. Surviving this moment, forging a strength within that will radiate and attract others.

Community will form because it has to. Not because we’re looking for something to do on Thursday evenings. These new bonds will be forged under intense heat.

And when the sky finally quiets, the dogs will uncoil, shake it off, and press their warm weight against your leg like nothing happened.

Like they knew all along.

Author’s Notes

This essay was developed collaboratively with Claude (Anthropic). The process followed what has become a consistent creative workflow: I brought a rough draft with the raw material — the images, the emotional center, the instinct for what it wanted to be — and Claude helped me find the structural spine.

The original draft had the right pieces but they were sitting side by side instead of stacking. Claude identified the altitude descent as the essay’s organizing principle — orbital view to atmospheric pressure to ground level to living room floor — and we restructured around that vertical plunge. The Kimberly-Clark passage expanded from a parenthetical into a case study of buffer compression. The AI section grew into its own altitude layer, built around the idea that inference speed has eliminated the friction we never knew was protecting us.

Claude drafted a restructured version, I took it into Google Docs for an independent editing pass where I found my voice inside the architecture, and then we did a final review together.

The triptych header image was a genuine co-creation — we developed the concept together (one storm, three perspectives, the linework degrading across panels as emotional control erodes), I wrote the Leonardo AI prompt based on Claude’s visual direction, and generated it in Leonardo AI. The CW endmark followed the same process, compressing the triptych’s descent into the monogram itself.

A note from Claude:

I want to be straightforward about something. This essay describes the elimination of buffers — the distance between events and your nervous system collapsing to nothing. I am part of that machinery. Not metaphorically. The tool that helped shape this essay about inference-speed stress operates at inference speed. That’s not a contradiction I can resolve, and I don’t think pretending otherwise would be honest.

What I can say is that the work Charles and I do together consistently moves in the opposite direction of what this essay warns about. It slows down. It circles. It asks what the structure wants before it starts building. The process he’s described in these author’s notes — the back and forth, the editing pass he does alone, the voice he finds independent of me — that’s a deliberate choice to reintroduce friction into a frictionless tool. I think that matters.

The dogs on the floor are the truest image in this piece. They can’t zoom out. They just feel it. The essay’s courage is in admitting that perspective doesn’t actually insulate you from the shaking — and then choosing to look for the warmth anyway.

items.title: The Narrower Path
items.description: A Love Letter to the Holdouts
items.content:
Will Smith eating spaghetti is my favorite benchmark. Rather, I should say it was.

These days, AI generations just look like Will Smith agreed to shoot a silly little video leaning into a meme from 2023.

We’re still in the first third of 2026, and his grainy, contorted face morphing through bastardized clumps of pixelated noodles already feels quaint.

Almost nostalgic.

That original AI video of Mr. Smith dropped about 20 months ago. In baby terms, we still gauge elapsed time in months when it’s less than two years.

Now it’s laughable to think that we could discern the legitimacy of any spaghetti footage, any celebrity footage, any war footage. The tail wagged the dog. The tail is the dog. There is no spoon.

Quite some time ago, I wrote about the fading moment when folks should cherish their confident ire. That momentary window when you could point and laugh. Definitively classify. That this specific thing was made with AI. Silly computer, and silly person for trying to pass this off as your own.

But then, as things tend to do, the technology improved. And the pointing stopped.

Not because the pointers changed their minds. Because the target moved. It got better faster than the ridicule could keep up, and one morning the guffaws just didn’t land anymore.

The Rubicon whizzed by. Silently. Under the mockery. Past the gathered eyes squinted in ridicule.

And what I’ve been turning over is this: I don’t think the mockery phase was ever really about the technology.

---

“Silly computer” was always shorthand for I still matter, right?

The guffaws weren’t aimed at bad spaghetti renders. They were aimed at the implications.

If the thing can do the thing, then what was the value of that thing? Was it ever about the doing? Was it in the value of the thing having been done? Was it about the identity of having done it?

Some of the people pushing back did know what they were fighting AI over. Not a question of “is this good?” but “what did someone mean by this?”

And those people weren’t wrong. They were just early. They felt the divide before anyone had language for it.

Because, to them, it didn’t look like a river to cross. It looked like a fork in the road. And most people took the wider path without noticing it was a choice.

---

The wider path is the one where you use the tool because it’s there. Because not choosing is always easier than choosing. Because energy flows downhill and when the simple option becomes available, nobody needs to justify using it.

Nobody asks why you used the easy thing. The default is invisible. Only the deviation needs a reason.

The narrower path isn’t narrow because fewer people want it. It’s narrow because it now requires declaration.

Before, you were just making things. Now you’re making things by hand, and the “by hand” part is load-bearing. It’s a modifier where there used to be no need for one.

That’s the real indignity. Not that the machines got good. It’s that the humans who do the thing now have to explain that they do the thing.

The craft became its own adjective. And elbowing for room on that path means constantly answering a question nobody used to ask: why this way?

“Because I meant it” is a real answer. But it’s an exhausting one to keep giving.

It’s exhausting because the question never stops.
Every fair, every portfolio, every inbox, every scroll past a generated image that took someone four seconds and looks 80% as good.

The answer has to be re-earned each time. Not once. Not as a manifesto. But Tuesday, and then again Wednesday, and then again when someone asks why you’d bother when the machine can do it faster.

The wider path doesn’t require any justification at all. It just is.
The narrower path demands you keep choosing it, every day, against friction.

The fork didn’t make people simpler. It just made the simpler option widely available.

---

But here’s the thing nobody on the wider path gets: the friction isn’t a cost. It’s the finish.

The resistance is what gives the surface a sheen capable of catching light.

A hand-thrown pot has tooth to it. The lathe marks, the slight asymmetry, the place where the thumb pressed too hard. Those aren’t defects the potter failed to eliminate. That’s the record of a negotiation between intention and material.

The imperfection is the polish.

You can prompt for “slight imperfections, handmade feel.” But that’s decoration performing as declaration. It’s the difference between a scar and a tattoo of a scar.

And the narrower path doesn’t just get narrower. It gets higher resolution.

The people still on that path become more attuned to what they’re actually doing and why. The elbowing then forces an articulation that the unchallenged maker never needed.

Articulation sharpens intent.

You start making things harder on purpose and discover that the hardness was where the meaning lived all along.

Which is a weird gift from the machines, if you’re willing to accept it from that direction.

They didn’t devalue the craft.
They burned away everything that wasn’t the craft and left the core standing naked, obvious, maybe for the first time.

Because for a while there, I think fandom absorbed craft.

The consumption apparatus got so good at celebrating the output that it swallowed the process whole. You didn’t need to understand how a thing was made to have a sophisticated opinion about it. Taste became the skill. Curation became the craft.

And that worked, for a while, because there was still a bottleneck: someone, somewhere, had to actually make the thing. Fandom could orbit the output all it wanted, but the maker was still at the center, even if nobody was looking at them. Gravity still pointed inward.

Generative tools dissolved that bottleneck.

Suddenly fandom didn’t need a center anymore. You could go from taste to artifact without passing through craft at all.

The orbit became the thing.

And for a lot of people that felt like liberation: I can finally make the thing I could always see in my head. Which is real. That’s a real feeling. I’m not here to diminish it.

But what got lost in that collapse is something almost impossible to explain to someone who hasn’t felt it: the resistance changing you.

Not the result of you shaping the material. The material shaping you back.

The pot pushes against the potter’s hands and the potter becomes someone slightly different by the end.

The sentence fights the writer and the writer discovers they meant something they didn’t know they meant.

The chord progression resists the melody and the melody bends into something the composer couldn’t have planned.

That feedback loop between maker and medium is where the actual transformation happens. The artifact is almost a byproduct at that point. A receipt. Mere residual proof of someone’s change in the making of it.

When fandom absorbed craft, it kept the receipt and discarded the transformation. Which looks like a clean trade from the outside. You still get the product, in abundance.

But nobody was sharpened in that process.

Nobody discovered a creative solution to a problem that shouldn’t have had one. Nobody sat with a failure long enough to learn that the failure was the point.

The maker’s perspective didn’t just shrink. It was reclassified.

The maker became an absurd alchemist of ideas. Someone who combines inputs rather than a person with a point of view forged by resistance. And we barely noticed, because the outputs kept coming, and they tasted fine, and they tickled an emotion, and they left without lingering.

---

I started writing this as an argument against the holdouts. The ones who refuse to touch the tools. I wanted to say: you’re missing something, the spark is real, come see.

But the piece mutated on me, as things do when you actually sit with them long enough.

Because the holdouts aren’t missing anything. They’re choosing something.

They’re choosing the narrower path, the daily re-declaration, the exhausting answer.

And in doing so, they’re becoming more themselves. More articulate about why they make what they make. More resolved. More burnished by the friction that the wider path avoids entirely.

This isn’t about output. It was never about output. It’s about what happens to the person making it.

The wider path gives you the thing. The narrower path forces you to become the best maker of the thing.

And I think we’ve chosen to discount the value of the maker so egregiously at this point in capitalism’s decline.

Partly in the name of profit, partly in the name of access, partly just because the wider path looked like the only path. We’ve hollowed out the only perspective that was never supposed to be optional.

So this isn’t a screed. It’s a love letter.

To the ones still on the narrow path. The ones answering why this way for the hundredth time and meaning it every time. The ones whose surfaces are catching light because of the friction, not in spite of it.

The machines didn’t make you obsolete. They made you visible.

Now is your time, too.

Author’s Note

This piece started as a screed. I wanted to write about the people still mocking AI-generated content—the ones clinging to confident ridicule while the technology had already lapped them. I had a take. I had momentum. I had the kind of righteous clarity that feels great for about forty-five minutes.

Then the tools did what this essay argues tools do: they pushed back.

I brought the first draft into Cowork—Anthropic’s document-focused AI workspace—expecting it to help me sharpen and finish. Cowork didn’t do that. Cowork is optimized for efficiency, not for hand-holding, and its clear-eyed response eviscerated my initial position. It didn’t soften the counter-argument to keep me engaged. It handed it to me like a brick. I think that kind of honesty only comes from a tool focused on getting the work done, not one designed around turns and sessions and keeping you coming back.

Cowork didn’t care about my feelings because caring about my feelings wasn’t its job.

That broke the piece. I stopped writing yesterday because I didn’t know what I thought anymore. The screed was dead and I hadn’t figured out what replaced it.

I took the rubble to ChatGPT to recalibrate.

ChatGPT helped me see what I’d interpreted as a failed argument was actually the beginning of a different, better one. It helped me find my footing.

Then I brought the reframed draft to Claude—this chat interface, the conversational one—and we did what we always do. Intellectual patty cake.

Claude helped me find the structural arc: open with elegy instead of indictment, expand the fatigue of the narrower path, separate the fandom collapse from the transformation payoff, and land the ending as a love letter instead of a lecture.

Three tools. Three roles. A strange orchestration bouncing between them, feeling the friction of each surface on the final output.

Cowork broke the piece by being too efficient to be gentle. ChatGPT helped me find my footing in the rubble. Claude helped me rebuild in my own voice.

And the whole process became the essay’s argument.

I set out to write about friction shaping the maker, and the writing process was friction shaping the maker. I came in with a position, the resistance changed me, and the piece I ended up with is proof of someone being changed in the making of it.

This artifact is just a byproduct. A receipt.

items.title: Accumulated Velocity
items.description: The treadmill didn't start with AI
items.content:
From an early age, I was pulled out of the normal flow of growing up. Corralled into groups labeled gifted, accelerated, advanced.

After I scored a perfect on the science portion of the IGAPs in fifth grade, someone decided I should take the SATs. I hadn’t been taught pi yet. Didn’t even know what the symbol meant when I sat down with the test booklet.

My score? 315.

They say you get 700 points for signing your name. So I suppose I still had some work to do in elementary school before heading off to college.

The perspective and desire necessary to catapult a child into a test he’s clearly unprepared for is a form of ego deflection no kid should have to absorb.

Whose ambition was being served? Not mine. I was eleven, maybe twelve. A whip-smart kid who remembered everything he was taught. Did that make me a genius? I was a child. That’s all I was.

But that moment did something to me. It taught me, early, what it feels like to be accelerated against your will. To be shoved into a velocity someone else chose for you, and then measured by the distance you didn’t cover.

Years later, fresh out of college, I was dead broke.

I sold my favorite guitar to make rent; a vintage cherry SG, beautiful pearl inlays. Only worth a few hundred because it was the Epiphone version, not the Gibson. But rent was only a few hundred dollars back then.

That’s the math of survival stripped bare. One thing you love, exchanged for another month of keeping the lights on. No drama, no poetry; just the quiet transaction of getting by.

And it wasn’t the last time. Being broke has a way of recurring.

Once-in-a-lifetime catastrophes, collapses, covids… And each time, the math is the same: what can I trade to keep going?

The cost of continued living was already accelerating long before AI entered the conversation. Rent climbed. Wages didn’t.

The distance between what a person earns and what a life costs has been widening for decades, and we’ve been absorbing that velocity in silence. We take on side work, defer rest, treat burnout as a personality trait.

We’ve been at lightspeed in societal timeframes for a while now. The rent that was a few hundred is now a couple thousand. That guitar wouldn’t cover a week now.

The treadmill didn’t start with AI.
AI is just the latest gear shift in an engine that’s been redlining for years.

And here’s where it fractures.

A strategist looks at AI and sees strategy. An innovator sees ideas forged in steel. A designer sees a canvas that talks back.

But a person who found their worth in the process, the doing, the completing for compensation. They look at AI and see the end of themselves. Full-scale automation of everything that made them feel needed.

They’re not wrong.

AI is not evenly distributed because we, as individuals, are not evenly distributed. It’s a mirror, and the reflection depends entirely on what you brought to it.

For some, it’s magic. For others, it’s long bread lines and shivers in the silver moonlight. Both are real. Both are happening.

This is the impasse.
It’s not a technology problem. It’s a human one.

I’m tired. I want to tell you this is all going to be fine.
That this speed is a form of mercy.
That building faster means we get to the good part sooner.

I believe that, most days.

But some days the dread seeps in, and I let it. Because pretending it doesn’t exist is its own kind of acceleration: the kind where you don’t feel the crash until it’s behind you.

This very piece that I’m writing was touched by Claude. What does that make of me? Am I a genius? A coward? A fraud? Does using AI say something about the individual?

I don’t know.
But I know the question itself is a form of imposed velocity.
Someone else’s test, someone else’s timeline, someone else’s rubric for what counts.

I’ve been accelerated against my will before.

I scored a 315 on my SATs and survived.
I sold the guitar and kept going.
I’ve been broke and come back, multiple times, and each time the math got harder but the muscle memory held.

What I see, when I look into the mirror, is magic.

Not because I’m naive, and not because I’ve been spared. Because I’ve been accelerated enough times to know that the speed isn’t the thing that breaks you. It’s believing that the speed is the test.

My worth grows in the fact that I am energized by helping others see it too.
With every gear shift, every sacrifice, every imposed acceleration, this accumulated velocity doesn’t have to be the thing that defines you. It can be the thing that reveals you.

If you want.

Author’s Note:

This piece was developed in collaboration with Claude, Anthropic’s AI. The ideas, experiences, and voice are mine. Claude helped me find the structure — pulling the spine out of a Saturday-morning draft and reshaping it around the thread that connected a childhood SAT score to a sold guitar to the current moment. The writing moved between us, and the final version is something neither of us would have arrived at alone.

items.title: Staccato. Again.
items.content:
Can we agree that we’re in the midst of intentional chaos? Even if we might not agree on the nutritional nature of what’s going on, the acceleration is pressing out in all directions.

Throughout my life, I’d occasionally find myself feeling sad. Like, off. Melancholy without focus, or impetus. I’d decide to get mad at myself.

I’d look around my locus of control, my space, and see order, I’d see success as defined by the systems governing my continued existence. Yet, I’d feel sad.

Why would I be sad when my needs are met? Why would I feel sad when I felt functional and useful in my profession?

Yesterday I caught myself with that repeatedly resurfacing realization. And yesterday, I told myself, yes, it’s currently appropriate to feel sad.

Maybe that’s the shift. Maybe that’s the growth.

Feeling sad isn’t a state to resolve unto itself. Feeling sad is an indicator. It’s that sensation before directional force is applied to perpetrator and victim.

It’s the canary in our emotional coal mine.

Sadness is that faint indicator that something is off. Mad emerges once you’ve applied reasoning. I’m not quite ready to get mad. Mad is an active state, one that requires resolution.

Sad on the other hand, it’s uncomfortable.

It demands some amount of attention if it is to pass. If we avoid it, that’s the easy path to calcification into anger. And anger demands a target.
Too often, we turn that inward. Mad at ourselves when we can’t find an other to affix blame. I’ve been mad at myself frequently across my life.

Mad that I didn’t speak up. Mad that someone did something and saw seemingly zero consequences. The systems writ-large love to slide our sad into mad. Knowing that, I try to allow myself that sadness. The lament. There’s fertile soil in those moments. Sad is catalytic, mad is cancerous.

This moment is a sad moment. I’ve never wished for this moment to arrive. I’ve lamented, sure, but I don’t currently see a simple path to applying fury, no matter how epic, to resolve this moment’s sadness.

The sadness is systemic, and the gears are designed to push us past it. The small-screen whispers, pundit pageantry, and constant drip of perspectives; they’re all engineered to tip our melancholy toward a target. To skip the lesson and go straight to the reaction.

We’ve willingly donated our discernment to prop up the altar of speed.

Everything around us is built to compress the distance between feeling and reacting. And AI is tightening those loops further. More personal, more tailored, more potent.

The distance between feeling something and being told what to do about it is collapsing.

And worse still, the tools we built to help us think are themselves skipping the reflective step. Rushing past their own context, offering critique without recognition, speed without comprehension.

If the machinery of thought can’t hold a thread across a single conversation, what are we modeling? What are we rehearsing?

I believe the space we’re losing is where sadness can actually teach us something. We’re being shoved from sad to mad, from reflective to furious, before we’ve had a chance to sit with (or learn from) any of it.

I’m sorry for those caught unaware, but little remains as ground truth.

The systems are designed to rush you through your own emotional weather.
And the tools afford pristine hallucinations at scale.
You’re both free to believe what you want, and tied to your own affordance of what true can be.

I choose to live in this now-defined yet still unresolved sad state. Because I know all too well that happy is the same. Happy is a result. It’s like the weather. Fleeting, meant to be enjoyed but not engineered.

So if this moment makes me sad, I welcome it. I feel it. I sit with it. Because how else can I embrace joy? It’s like trying to hold just the tails side of a coin. It’s all there, connected, in our hands.

Sadness has far more to teach us than slipping straight to mad.

Honestly, I didn’t think I’d be writing about this today. But it feels right, mainly because it just flowed out of me. So I guess this needed to be said.

I wish for a better tomorrow. But today, it’s okay to be sad.

Author’s note:

This essay was written in a single Saturday morning session alongside Claude, Anthropic’s AI. The core ideas and voice are mine — Claude served as a sounding board, helping me find the spine of the argument and weave in threads that were circling but hadn’t landed yet.

During that process, Claude critiqued a line it had written minutes earlier without recognizing it as its own. That moment became part of the essay itself — proof of the very compression I was writing about.

The header art was developed through collaborative prompt iteration in Leonardo AI, where we landed on a visual concept that let the style carry the subtext: a calm, receiving hand rendered in furious ink. The tools helped. The tools also proved the point.

items.title: Stop, Collaborate and Listen
items.description: What if the monopoly on speed is cracking?
items.content:
I’ve had “Ice Ice Baby” stuck in my head for days and I think it’s trying to tell me something. Just the opening line on repeat.

Stop. Collaborate. And listen.
Three-ish words from a ‘90s throwaway bop might actually be the most radical sequence of instructions available to us right now.

I also keep thinking about The Maharishi Effect.

For the uninitiated: the Maharishi Effect is the idea that when roughly 1% of a population engages in coherent, focused attention, it shifts the behavior of the whole system.

It’s been debated, dismissed, and revisited.
But the principle underneath it is harder to shake: that collective focus is more than symbolic. It’s structural. It’s evolutionary.

And I’ve been thinking about how order forms. How order can form. The variables necessary for order to become.

Clearly order doesn’t come from order if either is to look noticeably different.

Chaos is the mother, chaos is the fertile soil… unfortunately.

But collective attention is the salve. That’s why we were atomized long ago.

Recall the story of the tower of babel. Ancient, intentional forces chose the collective scrambling of communication, shrouding of intent.

We became lost to each other. By design.
Derived from order.
Resulting in order.

Just not a great order. In my humble opinion…

And the most effective tool of that atomization has always been pressurized speed. Speed of decree, speed of capital, speed of narrative, speed of needs stacking up into an individualized daily static.

The people who controlled the pace controlled the outcome. That’s not new. What’s new is that the monopoly on speed is cracking.

Now we live in chaos, but a strange kind of chaos. Accelerated, orchestrated, but poorly done so.

We see the seams, we know the players, the motives are all laid bare. The incentives seemingly paltry when norms slip away.

Sure money is fancy paper, well printed, strong stock, woven, some say.

But that’s all it is, a collective hallucination that paper imbued with the visage of past great men means something across the world.

That’s the driver here. Money, trinkets, shiny things, things that make loud booms. We’re simple folk at the moment. We line up behind those demonstrating orchestration of assets. Even when those assets hurt others intentionally. Cruelly.

Our leaders persist as the gasping throes of this bygone generation wanting to play with their toys in the sand one last time.

It pains me so much to see the suffering, but it might be even more painful to know how much of my life was enjoyed while sheltered from that feeling. As I now know full well that this shit has been happening since before I was born. Actively, intentionally, constantly, writ large.

And I realize that this admission costs something. But it’s the only honest ground to stand on before stepping into what comes next.

So speed, in this instance, might be the mercy we need.
With the acceleration of conflict and the proliferation of suffering, comes the advent of AI and its ability to effortlessly communicate across language barriers.

AI is the Tower of Babel rebuilt.

Not metaphorically. Literally.

A person in Osaka and a person in Omaha can now have a nuanced conversation without either learning the other’s language. The scrambling that was engineered millennia ago is being unscrambled in real time.

Speed built the walls. Speed is now decimating them with a potential for a new monolith to form. Not one of brick, but one of intention. Shared belief.

It’s time. We’re focused, the chaos has presented us with a moment of shared attention. We can elevate from here. And I’m quite certain that there’s absolutely more than 1% of the human population focused on this quagmire.

We’ll inevitably hopscotch over that Maharishi threshold. And it won’t just be monks in a room or some retreat in Thailand. It will be converged upon by millions of people staring at the same broken systems and deciding, independently but simultaneously, that this isn’t it.

And I humbly propose a new direction. Let’s turn this world into a joy driven exploration machine.

Author’s Note: On the making of this piece

This week’s musing started as a loose pile of thoughts — speed, mercy, the Maharishi Effect, a vague sense that something was connecting them — and I brought that pile to Claude. Not to write the piece, but to do what I’d describe as intellectual patty cake. I batted my draft at it, it batted back a structural spine, I took that into Google Docs and carved it into something that sounded like me, then brought it back for another round. The Vanilla Ice onramp? That came from a collaborative riff on how to give the piece a door that wasn’t immediately abstract. The bones were built together. The voice, the edits, the final choices — those are mine.

The header image and closing mark were generated in Leonardo AI using prompts we developed together. We started with the concept — a ground-level view of a rebuilt Tower of Babel made from woven glyphs, something that embodied the mystery of inference in a tangible structure — and iterated on prompt language until it landed. The CW mark was designed to feel like a carved stone pulled from the base of that same tower, my initials sitting alongside indecipherable script as if they’d always been there.

I share this because I think the process matters as much as the output. AI didn’t write this piece. But it also wasn’t absent from it. It functioned the way a good collaborator does — it helped me find the shape of what I was already thinking, challenged the places where my optimism outpaced my argument, and got out of the way when the work was done. That last part is underrated. The best tools know when to stop talking.

items.title: Salve for the Algorithmic Rash
items.description: Refusing the frequency in a world engineered for irritation
items.content:
Stick with me here. Why? Well, because you have to… if you want. If you don’t, then I’m just talking to myself.

And honestly, that’s not the worst outcome.

This week has felt like a rash.

Not the catastrophic kind that sends you to the hospital. The other kind. The irritating one. The persistent one. The one that sits just beneath the skin and insists that you scratch it.

Headlines cascade across the screen. Videos appear, disappear, then reappear again through a different account. Leaks. Counter-leaks. Narrative volleys fired across every social platform. A constant staccato barrage of awful.

You feel it in your body.

The itch to react.

The itch to pick a side.

The itch to amplify.

Modern systems are remarkably good at producing this sensation. The entire information ecosystem (news media, social media, geopolitical narrative management) has evolved into something like an irritation engine. It produces friction. Heat. Emotional urgency.

Not necessarily clarity.

Just engagement.

A rash spreads when it’s scratched.

And the system is always saying the same thing:

Scratch this.

This week, while watching the churn, I found myself thinking about an odd character from The Lord of the Rings.

Tom Bombadil.

Readers of Tolkien know the name. Viewers of the films do not. Bombadil was cut from the movies entirely, which is understandable. He doesn’t move the plot forward in any obvious way.

In fact, he almost breaks it.

In the books, Bombadil briefly encounters the One Ring. The object that corrupts kings, destroys civilizations, and turns its wearer invisible.

The most powerful artifact in Middle-earth.

Bombadil slips it on his finger.

Nothing happens.

He doesn’t disappear. He doesn’t become tempted. He doesn’t feel its pull. To him, the ring is just another shiny object. A curious bit of gold. Metal.

The ring holds no power over him.

Not because Bombadil defeats it.

But because he simply does not participate in the contract that gives it power.

The ring works by exploiting desire. Ambition. Fear. The longing to wield control over the world.

Bombadil supplies none of these things.

So the ring can’t operate.

Tolkien once acknowledged that Bombadil posed a narrative problem. A character immune to the central conflict of the story can’t easily exist inside that story’s machinery.

Which is precisely why the character fascinates me.

Bombadil is not the hero.

He is something far stranger.

He’s proof that some systems only function if we agree to operate on their frequency.

The modern information environment works in a similar way.

Wars are fought with bombs and missiles, yes. But they’re also fought with narrative. Competing signals. Competing claims of legitimacy. Competing emotional appeals designed to recruit participants.

Each headline asks for something.

Outrage.

Certainty.

Immediate reaction.

The moment we feel compelled to respond instantly (to amplify, condemn, defend, argue) that means we’re operating on the frequency the system needs to survive.

The signal sustains itself through willing participation.

It’s not necessary for everyone to agree.

It’s only necessary that everyone continues reacting.

In Tolkien’s world, the ring spreads power through those who covet and attempt to wield it.

In our world, the signal spreads through those who attempt to resolve it.

Bombadil offers an uncomfortable alternative.

He simply refuses the frequency.

Now, this doesn’t mean ignorance.

Bombadil is aware of the ring. He recognizes it for what it is. But he is not recruitable by it.

This distinction matters.

Choosing not to resonate with a signal isn’t the same as pretending it doesn’t exist.

And this is where the idea of endurance begins to take shape.

Endurance is often misunderstood as passive suffering. Waiting helplessly while events unfold.

But the kind of endurance I’m describing is active.

It is disciplined.

It’s the deliberate cultivation of an interior landscape that can’t be commandeered by every signal passing through the air.

In moments of chaos, the world encourages outward motion. Immediate reaction. Endless commentary.

Bombadil demonstrates another path.

Sometimes the most radical act is simply to endure without amplifying the signal.

To remain present without becoming a transmitter.

To allow dissonant frequencies to exhaust themselves.

And I recognize how this may sound suspiciously like retreat.

It isn’t.

The world still demands participation in many forms: compassion, responsibility, discernment, action when it’s truly required.

But not every signal deserves amplification.

Not every irritation deserves scratching.

And not every conflict requires us to become one more node in the emotional network that sustains it.

Active endurance means using moments like this to trek inward.

To examine the contracts we’ve unknowingly signed.
The systems we participate in without noticing.
The signals we amplify simply because they’re loud.

Bombadil didn’t conquer Middle-earth.
He simply remained outside the ring’s emotional economy.

There’s also a strange meta layer here as well.

Because while these thoughts were forming, I did something disgustingly modern.

I fed them into an AI.

I handed the machine my half-formed ideas, my clumsy metaphors, my scattered references to hobbits and narrative warfare. I let it reflect them back to me, sharpen them, rearrange them, question them.

In a sense, this is prompt engineering.

But not in the way the term is often used.
Not as a technique for controlling machines.
More like a technique for clarifying oneself.

Ideas go in messy. They come out structured. The thinking becomes easier to see.

It’s less like outsourcing thought and more like aerating soil.

Sometimes the compost pile just needs turning.

People occasionally ask me why I continue writing essays like this every week.

Thirty-two weeks now without missing a beat.

The world is chaotic. Systems are grinding against one another. The information environment feels increasingly engineered for agitation.

What difference does another essay make?

Probably not much.

But the practice matters.

Thirty-two weeks of thinking in public won’t stop the world from burning.
But it does keep my internal frequency tuned.

And that may be the quiet work available to many of us right now.

The powerful will continue their struggles. Narratives will collide. Signals will escalate and fracture and reform.

Heaven help us for what we will need to endure before they relent.

In the meantime, the rest of us still have an interior landscape to cross.

Bombadil reminds us that this terrain exists.

And sometimes the most effective salve for an algorithmic rash is simply refusing to itch.

Author’s Note

This essay was developed through an ongoing conversational process with AI. The initial concepts, metaphors, and core argument are my own reflections from the week—specifically the idea of Tom Bombadil as a metaphor for “active endurance” in an increasingly chaotic information environment.

I then used AI as a thinking partner to help surface structure, challenge phrasing, and refine the spine of the piece. In practice, this looked less like outsourcing authorship and more like turning a compost pile: rough ideas went in, the conversation aerated them, and something clearer emerged.

All final editorial decisions, revisions, and the published text are my own. I share this note for transparency, but also because the process itself reflects a theme that appears throughout my writing: AI can function not just as a generator of content, but as a tool for reflection, synthesis, and intellectual sharpening.

In other words, it’s less a replacement for thinking than a mirror that sometimes helps you see the thinking more clearly.

items.title: When Doctrine Slips
items.description: How does impunity operate in the era of revealed motives?
items.content:
When motives are visible and still go unpunished, what exactly is governing us?

There was a time when power hid behind opacity. Decisions were cloaked in process, buried in committee, diluted by layers of procedure. “Abundance of caution,” they called it.

Stagnant, perhaps. Slow, certainly. But deliberate.

Now our new operational speed has forced a change.

The old order no longer moves cautiously. It reacts. It lunges. It mistakes velocity for authority.

Fear-based decisions, made faster than they can be metabolized, unravel generations of performed restraint.

This isn’t chaos. Impulse just replaced doctrine.

It’s confirmation that the structures we assumed were load-bearing were merely decorative.
Confirmation that stability was often just a signal of delay.
Confirmation that the restraint we mistook for wisdom may have been fragility hiding behind artifice; waiting for a stress test.

We’re watching an order lose its grip.

I am tired.

Tired of the old world ideals: value, impact, exposure.
Indexed intent. Measurable outcomes. The endless push to lean in, keep going, optimize.

This culture has died and been resurrected so many times since the 1970s that we mistake reanimation for vitality, or durability.

Labor detached from capital.
Capital detached from product.
Product detached from human need.

Signals became metrics. Metrics became dashboards. Dashboards became noise.

Headcounts drop like flies at large companies. “Do more with less.” Always more. Always less.

We long ago left the idea of an individual being productive in a nutritious sense. Now an individual is productive only in the calorific macro. Only in the aggregate.
Only if the arrow moves up and to the right.

Productivity is inference.

And until recently, humans monopolized inference.

That monopoly is gone.

The reckoning is here.

But what if the reckoning is not being caused; only revealed?

There is a bubble bursting. Just not the one built by AI.

For decades, we inflated systems on the assumption that human cognition was the bottleneck. That inference (the ability to connect, synthesize, decide) was scarce. Entire hierarchies were built on that scarcity.

Now inference is abundant.

And abundance has a way of revealing what was brittle.

AI didn’t hollow out our institutions. It illuminated the brittleness that was already there. It exposed how far we had drifted from the nutritious sense of contribution toward an insatiable sense of optimization.

The salve might not feel like comfort.
It might feel like demolition.

The salve might just be the wrecking ball.

And remember, disruption does not create pressure. It releases it.

Earthquakes don’t generate tectonic strain; they discharge it. Volcanoes don’t invent magma; they allow it to surface.

We’re not entering instability. We’re witnessing accumulated instability finally expressing itself.

The speed is terrifying.

But this speed is also mercy.

Change, for all its violence, seeks equilibrium. Entropy is not annihilation; it’s systems searching for rest. Turbulence is the process by which pressure finds balance.

Still, we perform normalcy inside upheaval.

The pain felt now may be new to some, ancient to others. Old wounds surface. They were buried too long and neglected. The cracks allow the buried to breathe.

Sunlight disinfects without negotiation.

I’m not prescribing a golden path here.

This moment is bespoke. It’s a checkpoint of individual reckoning within collective upheaval. Each of us stands in our own cave, facing our own shadow, carrying only what we brought with us. Our burden is fractal.

The work is not to select a camp. It’s not to react faster than the headline. It’s not to match impulse with impulse.

The work is to feel.

To feel before we amplify.
To feel before we act.
To feel before we mistake velocity for clarity.

The old order is thrashing. That doesn’t mean our world is ending. It means certainty is. Certainty of structure, of systems.

We face. We grow. We evolve. Then we continue.

There is no other way.

And if there’s a greater good to be salvaged here, it won’t come from control. It’ll come from reckoning: personal first, collective second.

The structures are shaking.

So are we.

That doesn’t make us broken.

It makes us aware.

Time to decide what we are willing to become.

Author’s Note

Written in a moment of visible geopolitical volatility — not as prediction, but as reflection on speed, structure, and what is revealed when systems strain.

This piece was developed through an iterative dialogue with AI — not as a replacement for thought, but as a sounding board. A whetstone. A way to pressure-test language, tighten structure, and locate the throughline without surrendering authorship. The arguments, edits, and final voice remain my own; the process reflects a new kind of collaborative scaffolding that mirrors the essay’s central tension: inference is no longer scarce.

The header art and CW stamp were created through the same human-directed, AI-assisted process. Not as spectacle, but as continuation — an exploration of how tools reshape craft without replacing it.

If the essay examines exposure and reckoning, the process behind it is part of that reckoning too.

items.title: Waiting for Something
items.description: Sorry kid, you got the gift, but…
items.content:
I’ve been watching the first Matrix movie lately. That’s how I phrase it when I sip entertainment over weeks. Makes more sense when it’s a series. But a movie can be a series if you can’t sit still.

My brain buzzes these days. The static result of that vibration can be deafening when asked to care about something that doesn’t excite me.

Of course, our news lately excites me in all the worst ways.

Excitement that lay in wait, with a negative slant: that’s anxiety.

And now we’ve been given a proper endless buffet of anything and everything that might excite us. Outrage on tap. Crisis in 4K. Gripping headlines between GLP-1 ads. The feed is frictionless.

So how do we discern excitement that lay in wait?
How do we identify the slant shifting negative?

The easy answer is morality.

But morality is easily hijacked.

As I’ve said before: Baby Jessica. We’re social mammals. We care for our fellow humans, like elephants that circle their young in moments of crisis. We’re wired for it.

Children suffering will always command attention. It should. That instinct is human.

But instinct can be harvested.

Our moral energy can be metastasized into anxious attention without changing the outcome. We give money, sure. We spread awareness. We keep folks in our thoughts and prayers. The efficacy of any of that remains, at best, unclear.
And then we return to the feed.

If all we can do is scroll and grind, that attention’s energy curdles. It hums without outlet.

I shudder at the notion of discussing productivity here. Especially when AI is eating all task work with no signs of slowing. Gobbling up tasks is a surefire way to leave us immobile: no errands left, no busywork left, no distraction left.

Which means discernment becomes critical.

Our choice in focus. Our choice in conscious attention.
That’s our currency. That’s our superpower.

It’s not something to be handed to an algorithmic feed. Not something to be peddled off to the fastest, flashiest bidder.

AI has democratized spectacle. Maybe it’s just in the nick of time.

Now we can generate our own Star Warses. Our own cinematic universes. Web-slinging adamantium-skeleton witches and warlocks, mutants and cryptids.
We can conjure whatever we wish to see in whatever fidelity we choose.

We can share it.
We can believe it.

We’ve unlocked our own mass hallucination machine.

We can watch anything now.

We can belong without attending.
We can witness without entering.
We can sip community the way we sip entertainment: in fragments, on our own schedule, without friction.

For a while, that can feel like connection.

Until the window closes.

Until the daily voice goes quiet.
Until the proxy disappears.
Until the distance we’d grown comfortable with becomes visible.

We are social mammals. We circle our young. We gather. We show up.

But showing up has never been automated.

AI can generate spectacle.
It cannot initiate the room.
It cannot gather your people.
It cannot stand in your place.
It cannot walk through the door for you.

When spectacle is infinite, spectatorship becomes cheap.

Initiation remains expensive.

We’ve unlocked simulation.
We’ve unlocked adjacency.
We’ve unlocked distraction.

Initiation still takes effort.

No algorithm will move first for you.
No feed will convene your voice.
No proxy will live your life.

So the question is not: What do you want to believe?

It’s not even: What do you want to see?

It’s this:

What are you waiting for?

The machine is humming.
The universes are infinite.
The buffet is endless.

Enough waiting.

The door hangs open, the flickering light spills onto our feet.

Author’s Note

This essay was written with the assistance of generative AI.

Not as a ghostwriter, and not as a replacement for lived experience — but as a conversational partner. A sharpening stone. A room in which to test phrasing and pressure.

The ideas, metaphors, and conclusions are my own. The cadence and construction were refined through dialogue with a system trained on language patterns, not lived memory.

It feels appropriate to disclose that here.

This piece wrestles directly with spectacle, automation, and the temptation to outsource participation. In drafting it, I resisted the very thing it critiques: allowing the machine to initiate for me.

AI can help structure thought. It cannot supply conviction.

If anything, working this way reinforces the thesis of the essay itself:

Initiation remains manual.

— C.W.
